Specifically, the inverse Simpson’s index is used to determine the number of cells that can be drawn from a neighbor list before one batch is observed twice. Thus, LISI scores range from 1 to N, where N is the total number of batches in the dataset. Typically, neighborhood lists to compute LISI scores are extracted from weighted kNN graphs with k = 90 nearest neighbors at a fixed perplexity of p = 1 3 k. These nearest neighbor graphs are constructed using Euclidean distances on PCA or other embeddings. In contrast, integrated graphs that are output by methods such as Conos or BBKNN typically contain far fewer than k = 90 neighbors. Running LISI metrics with differing numbers of nearest neighbors per node results in differing sensitivities per neighborhood and thus skews any comparison with graph-based integration outputs.
